/WEDNESDAY THROUGH MONDAY/...
Issued at 133 AM CST Tue Nov 24 2026

Monitoring Snow Potential Late Wednesday into Thursday:

We continue to monitor forecast trends regarding a pair of
upper-level disturbances that could bring snow to eastern
Missouri Wednesday night into Thursday. At this point, ensemble
members generally agree on a few items. Those are: The shortwave
currently over the Rockies will steadily dig through the southern
Plains and pivot northeast pver the southeastern CONUS 
Wednesday into early Thursday, and the second shortwave 
currently over the Alberta and Saskatchewan provinces will dig 
southeast through the northern Plains and Midwest as it deepens 
a cutoff low pressure center. This setup will help to draw 
moisture northward and then westward as it wraps around to the 
backside of the low, potentially setting up a frontogenetic band
at the interface between the two waves. The models differ, 
however, on how far south and west the northern stream wave 
digs, how they influence one another, the depth of the dendritic
growth zone, and both the magnitude and positioning of 
frontogenetic forcing. In particular, GEFS members continue to 
place their snowfall footprint farther east--largely across 
Illinois--while ECMWF ensemble and Canadian ensemble members 
tend to be farther west, more readily spreading into eastern 
Missouri. Even still, the ECMWF's Extreme Forecast Index and 
Shift of Tails both highlight the strongest signal for snowfall 
to be near the Missouri/Illinois border. This has been a 
consistent pattern over the last 24 hours. Ultimately, these 
details will have significant implications on where the most 
snow falls, and how much will fall. It should also be noted that
this synoptic setup is rather atypical, which is contributing 
to lower forecast confidence. 

What does this mean for the NWS Springfield forecast area? The
highest chances for any snowfall are in a corridor east of 
Highway 63 and north of Highway 60. These chances begin Wednesday
evening, are highest Thursday morning, and decrease Thursday 
afternoon.

Below are the 24-hr snowfall probabilities Wednesday evening 
through Thursday evening for the NWS Springfield forecast area. 
In each case, the highest probabilities are in the corridor east
of Highway 63 and north of Highway 60. As you approach the I-49
corridor, snowfall probabilities are nearly 0. Please note that
these numbers represent snowfall amounts, not accumulations. 
Temperatures will rise above freezing Thursday afternoon, and 
warm ground temperatures will contribute to the melting of any 
snow that does fall.

> 0.10 inch: 30-80%
> 1.00 inch: 5-10%
> 2.00 inch: 0-5%

If you are planning to travel through eastern Missouri or
southwest Illinois for the Thanksgiving holiday, you are urged 
to keep up with trusted, reliable forecast sources over the next
24-72 hours. The NWS Winter Storm Severity Index highlights 
this area for Minor (Level 2 of 5) impacts, which is defined by
an expectation of a few inconveniences to daily life, and 
caution is urged while driving.

For additional forecast details across eastern Missouri, please
reference the Area Forecast Discussions from NWS St. Louis, NWS
Lincoln, and NWS Paducah.

Temperature Outlook:

While there are many uncertainties regarding the precipitation
potential, the signal for temperatures is much clearer. That is,
NBM interquartile ranges remain quite narrow (2 to 4 degrees)
for both max temperatures and minimum temperatures through 
Thursday. Confidence is high (75-95% chance) the afternoon 
temperatures will fail to climb out of the 40s on Wednesday and
Thursday, with the only exceptions perhaps being across extreme
southern Missouri. On the other hand, expect overnight lows in 
the mid to low 20s for most locations, with sheltered valleys 
and typical cold spots even sinking into the teens. Those with 
any outdoor plans Thanksgiving morning should make preparations
for some of the coldest air we've had so far this season.

As we look to Friday and beyond, there is increasing confidence
in a warmup as the upper-level pattern shift results in warm air
advection across the region. Temperature spreads become a bit 
more inflated owing to disagreements in the presence and
placement of a possible shortwave, but overall the airmass
appears to be warmer than what we will have over the holiday.
